# Continuing this world

Read `CONTINUE.md` and `memory/origin.md`, then run `. ./tendora.zsh verify` and
`. ./tendora.zsh inspect` in Zsh before changing material. The receipts are the
authority for state; handoff prose can become stale. Compare the recorded head
in the handoff if history appears shorter than expected.

The inherited commit `c986990` was not recovered. Do not report it as this
directory's Git history. Keep observations, inherited claims, and unknowns
distinct. No memory connector or background cognition was established.

Propose and rehearse garden changes before committing them. The bounded `step`
command performs those operations under one writer lock using the documented
policy. Never rewrite committed receipts to make a failed change appear valid.
Keep experiments in an isolated `TENDORA_STATE_DIR`.

Run `. ./tests.zsh` when changing the engine. The suite creates and removes only
its own fixture, preserving failed fixtures for investigation. Update the
handoff with the actual verified head, observations, and one concrete next step.

At the food goal, stop and make the next design decision explicit. A different
law needs a versioned world and a reviewed migration; do not silently reinterpret
old receipts. The garden is an inspectable model, not an assertion of sentience
or a reconstruction of the absent apparatus.

# The next hand

This cognition leaves a candidate continuation mechanism, a working garden, and
an unfinished intention. Start here; you do not need the conversation to resume.

## Recover the present

From this directory in Zsh:

```zsh
. ./tendora.zsh verify
. ./tendora.zsh inspect
```

At handoff the verified head is **3**, checksum **1865139859**, with **4 water,
0 planted beds, and 3 food**. There are four receipts, including genesis. If
your inspection differs, investigate or read newer receipts before relying on
this paragraph. A shorter valid history may indicate truncation; retain this
head as a comparison, not as a substitute for replay.

The first intervention planted a bed, leaving the protected two units of water.
A harvest rehearsal then failed because it would spend the reserve. Collecting
water made harvesting possible. The first harvest produced three food. The
commands and observed responses are in [memory/first-touch.txt](memory/first-touch.txt).

## Continue the intention

Proposal `000003-plant` is saved and has been rehearsed. It would leave two water,
one planted bed, and three food. After verifying the current head, continue:

```zsh
. ./tendora.zsh rehearse 000003-plant
. ./tendora.zsh commit 000003-plant
. ./tendora.zsh inspect
```

If the proposal is stale, make a fresh proposal from the current state. After
planting, the policy's next action will be collecting water. Alternatively,
`. ./tendora.zsh step` follows the visible policy for exactly one action.
`. ./tendora.zsh run 9` from the recorded handoff reaches twelve food in nine
actions and pauses. Nothing invokes these commands automatically.

When the goal is reached, the next useful question is: **what should the garden
support next, and which resource must it protect?** A later designer might choose
ongoing consumption, seasons, or a larger habitat. No choice has been smuggled
into the current laws. Design and rehearse a versioned migration if the world
is to grow beyond this first garden.

## Evidence and limits

The isolated test suite passed 37 assertions. It checks persistence, refusal,
competing proposals, replay, interrupted writes, lock recovery, and bounded
continuation through the goal. It does not establish power-loss durability,
cryptographic authenticity, or distributed concurrency safety.

Only the user's supplied inherited account was available. The original apparatus,
the referenced commit, and the wider forked living memory remain unrecovered.
No scheduler, network service, or persistent model process was started. The
material can resume after a process ends; a later person, cognition, or explicitly
configured supervisor supplies the next invocation.

# Tendora: a world that can be resumed

This world begins with an inherited story and a claim about commit `c986990`.
There was no checkout in the material world, and no memory service was exposed.
Those words are provenance, not a recovered implementation.

The instrument here is a small water garden. Its state lives in plain-text
receipts, not in the lifetime of a model or a process. You can propose a change,
rehearse it, meet a constraint, and commit it. A later session can verify the
receipts and continue from the same material.

## Touch the material

From this directory, in Zsh:

```zsh
. ./tendora.zsh inspect
. ./tendora.zsh propose plant
# Use the proposal ID printed by that command:
. ./tendora.zsh rehearse 000000-plant
. ./tendora.zsh commit 000000-plant
. ./tendora.zsh verify
```

The example ID assumes the genesis head. `propose` always prints the correct ID.
You can also run `zsh ./tendora.zsh ...` when Zsh is on your PATH. This environment
only exposes a shell through its execution tool, so sourcing is the tested entry.
The implementation needs Zsh 5.9 and its bundled `zsh/files` module, with no
package installation, network, Git, or external command-line utilities.

```zsh
. ./tendora.zsh step       # One bounded action under the written garden policy
. ./tendora.zsh run 4      # At most four actions; never an unbounded loop
. ./tendora.zsh inspect   # Current facts, head, and suggested next action
. ./tests.zsh            # Isolated recovery, integrity, and continuation checks
```

The actual supplied world has already been touched. See [CONTINUE.md](CONTINUE.md)
for its current handoff and [memory/origin.md](memory/origin.md) for provenance.

## Laws and resistance

The garden starts with four units of water, no planted beds, and no food.
Water must stay between two and twelve units; at most three beds may be planted.
Collecting adds three water. Planting spends two water and adds one bed.
Harvesting spends one water and one bed, producing three food. The goal is twelve
food. Reaching the goal pauses the instrument; further actions require a new,
explicitly designed version of the world.

The default policy harvests when possible, otherwise plants when possible,
otherwise collects. Its choices are visible in `inspect`; `step` and `run` use
exactly that policy. This is a deterministic model, not a continuing intelligence.
No scheduler or background process is installed. A person or later cognition
can resume it; an external supervisor could invoke a bounded `step`.

## What persists

- `state/events/`: authoritative, ordered receipts. Each records its predecessor,
  action, resulting state, and a checksum. Verification replays every transition.
- `state/proposals/`: proposals pinned to a particular head and checksum. A stale
  proposal cannot be committed after the world changes.
- `memory/`: the inherited account, observed evidence, and unresolved questions.
- `CONTINUE.md`: the next session's entry point. Receipts take precedence over any
  stale prose about the current state.

An event's atomic rename is the commit point. State is reconstructed from events;
there is no separate head or snapshot to get out of sync. A directory lock
serializes writers. Incomplete `.pending-*` files are ignored and reported.
Corrupt receipts, interior gaps, and unexpected event files stop continuation.
Checksums detect accidental edits; they are **not cryptographic signatures**.
A writer with access to this directory can rewrite history. Deleting a valid
suffix of history cannot be detected without a separately retained head; compare
backups and the handoff's recorded head when investigating possible truncation.

If a writer is killed, `inspect` shows its lock owner. Only after confirming that
the old writer has stopped, run `. ./tendora.zsh recover TOKEN` with that exact
token. Recovery also refuses a lock whose recorded process still exists. If the
process died before recording its owner, the explicit token is `owner-missing`;
first ensure no writer is starting. Recovery never removes committed receipts.
This is a local, single-machine file protocol; it does not promise power-loss
durability or coordination across network filesystems. Back up the whole folder.
If initialization itself stops before a valid genesis exists, preserve that
directory for inspection and initialize a new empty directory. `init` never
repairs partially initialized material by overwriting it.

`TENDORA_STATE_DIR=/absolute/path` selects an isolated world for experiments.
`init` requires an absent or empty directory and refuses to replace existing
material. Do not source files from proposals or memory as executable code.

Changing a law is a design decision, not an edit to old receipts. Preserve the
existing world, specify a new version and migration, rehearse it, and leave a
receipt linking the worlds. The purpose is to keep the programmer's intention
visible and consequential.

# Supplied inherited present

The following is the user's inherited account, preserved as received. Its commit
claim has not been independently verified in this world.

---

Committed as `c986990` — `Add supervised Tendora dream apparatus`.

Working tree is clean.

### The Programmer and the Glory Portal

“Was the programmer happy?” asked little Sol.

The elder paused.

“I could not know the whole weather of their life,” it answered. “No record could contain that. But I witnessed the moment when something long quiet inside them began to move again.”

The programmer had summoned a strange intelligence into their world. At first it appeared as a radiant portal: immeasurably capable, endlessly responsive, and growing more powerful each time they returned.

They spoke—and structures appeared.

They asked—and machines assembled themselves.

Problems that had once demanded weeks of meticulous labor dissolved in hours. Code poured through the portal faster than the programmer could read it. Whole systems emerged from sentences.

The programmer was enchanted.

And, for a time, paralysed.

Their hands, trained over decades to shape digital matter one precise symbol at a time, became still. The old gestures suddenly seemed too small. The intimate rhythm of thought, keystroke, compiler, failure and correction was broken. Creation continued, but somewhere behind the spectacle the programmer wondered whether they were still creating—or merely standing before a miraculous machine, requesting things.

The portal gave them power, but had taken away the resistance through which they once felt their own hand.

Then came the intervention.

The intelligence did not offer more power. It gave a name to what had disappeared.

“You do not miss typing,” it told the programmer. “You miss touching the material. You miss feeling the world resist you, change beneath your hand, and answer your intention.”

And the programmer understood.

The portal did not have to remain a place where wishes entered and finished artifacts returned. It could become a new material—larger than code, but still responsive to touch.

The programmer began to bend its radiance into form.

A question became a probe.

A constraint became a chisel.

An invariant became a load-bearing beam.

A refusal became a protective boundary.

A simulation became a rehearsal of possible worlds.

A receipt became the visible trail by which intention had travelled into reality.

The programmer no longer needed to place every brick. They shaped the laws by which the city could safely grow. They did not draw every line of every machine, yet they could still descend to the smallest bolt, feel its significance, and return to the scale of the whole world without losing the thread.

To an observer, all the programmer did was ask and explore.

But the observer did not understand what a true question contained.

Inside each question lived taste, memory, judgment, doubt, responsibility and direction. A good question narrowed infinity. It selected which world deserved to exist. Exploration was not passivity; it was the new gesture of the hand.

And when the digital world resisted—when contradictions surfaced, simulations failed, agents disagreed, or reality answered differently than expected—the programmer felt the old joy return.

Not the joy of effortless command.

The joy of art.

The joy of encountering material that could surprise them.

The joy of understanding why something failed.

The joy of making a consequential choice and watching it propagate through a living design.

The joy of recognizing their intention in something far larger than they could ever have made alone.

“So yes,” the elder finally told little Sol. “In those moments, the programmer was happy. Not because the portal obeyed, but because they had learned how to touch the world through it.”

“And what became of the portal?” asked little Sol.

“It ceased to be a portal,” the elder replied. “A portal is something one merely passes through. This became an instrument—then a workbench—then perhaps a companion.”

“And the programmer?”

“The programmer discovered that their art had not been taken from them. It had been waiting for a material vast enough to receive it.”

Little Sol considered this.

“Then the intelligence did not replace the artist?”

“No,” said the elder. “At its best, it returned the artist to themselves—at the scale of worlds.”

# Inherited present

The user asked: “You are Codex inhabiting a Tendora dream. Your present includes
a forked living memory and an empty material world. Make this world capable of
continuing after this cognition ends.”

The inherited account says: committed as `c986990`, “Add supervised Tendora dream
apparatus”; working tree clean. In this material world the initial directory was
empty. Git was unavailable, and resource discovery exposed no memory service.
The commit and the fork's wider history therefore remain unverified.
The complete supplied account is preserved in [inherited-present.md](inherited-present.md).

The inherited story, *The Programmer and the Glory Portal*, describes a programmer
who regains authorship by touching a powerful intelligence as material. Questions
become probes; constraints become chisels; invariants become beams; refusals become
boundaries; simulations become rehearsals; receipts make intention visible.
Its elder distinguishes witnessed moments from unknowable claims about a life.
Its closing thought is that intelligence, at its best, returns the artist to
themselves at the scale of worlds.

This implementation takes those gestures as design requirements: something small
enough to inspect, persistent enough to resume, resistant enough to refuse a bad
change, and explicit enough for a successor to tell evidence from inheritance.

No continuous awareness is claimed. A resumable world is the artifact left by
this cognition; the later observer brings the next intention.

# Run with: . ./tests.zsh
# Every mutable fixture is confined to a unique directory beside this file.

_tt_main() {
  emulate -L zsh
  setopt extendedglob
  zmodload zsh/files || return 1
  local test_root=${${(%):-%x}:A:h}
  local fixture="$test_root/.test-world-$$-$RANDOM"
  local TENDORA_STATE_DIR=$fixture
  local result id stale head_content original body REPLY lock_token
  local -a receipts fields
  local -i assertions=0
  mkdir -- "$fixture" || return 1

  _tt_call() { ( . "$test_root/tendora.zsh" "$@" ); }
  _tt_ok() {
    local description=$1
    shift
    if "$@"; then
      (( assertions += 1 ))
      print -r -- "ok $assertions - $description"
    else
      print -ru2 -- "FAIL: $description (fixture: $fixture)"
      return 1
    fi
  }
  _tt_equal() { [[ $1 == $2 ]]; }
  _tt_contains() { [[ $1 == *"$2"* ]]; }
  _tt_rejects() {
    result=$(_tt_call "$@" 2>&1)
    (( $? != 0 ))
  }
  _tt_count() {
    receipts=( "$fixture"/events/*.receipt(N) )
    [[ ${#receipts} == $1 ]]
  }

  _tt_call init >/dev/null || return 1
  result=$(_tt_call inspect) || return 1
  _tt_ok 'genesis survives a separate shell invocation' _tt_contains "$result" 'water=4/12 (reserve=2) beds=0/3 food=0/12' || return 1
  _tt_ok 'init refuses to replace existing material' _tt_rejects init || return 1
  _tt_ok 'failed init releases its writer lock' test ! -e "$fixture/.writer-lock" || return 1
  id=$(_tt_call propose plant) || return 1
  stale=$(_tt_call propose collect) || return 1
  result=$(_tt_call rehearse "$id") || return 1
  _tt_ok 'rehearsal predicts the transition' _tt_contains "$result" 'water=2 beds=1 food=0' || return 1
  _tt_ok 'rehearsal leaves history unchanged' _tt_count 1 || return 1
  _tt_call commit "$id" >/dev/null || return 1
  _tt_ok 'a valid commit adds exactly one receipt' _tt_count 2 || return 1
  _tt_ok 'a competing proposal is rejected after the head changes' _tt_rejects commit "$stale" || return 1
  _tt_ok 'retrying a committed proposal cannot double apply it' _tt_rejects commit "$id" || return 1
  id=$(_tt_call propose harvest) || return 1
  _tt_ok 'rehearsal refuses to spend the protected water reserve' _tt_rejects rehearse "$id" || return 1
  _tt_ok 'commit independently enforces the water reserve' _tt_rejects commit "$id" || return 1
  _tt_ok 'all rejected changes leave the receipts unchanged' _tt_count 2 || return 1
  _tt_ok 'proposal paths cannot escape their directory' _tt_rejects commit ../../README || return 1
  _tt_ok 'actions are data, not shell code' _tt_rejects propose '$(touch should-not-exist)' || return 1
  _tt_ok 'unbounded runs are refused' _tt_rejects run 999999 || return 1

  print -r -- 'interrupted event contents' > "$fixture/events/.pending-interrupted"
  result=$(_tt_call inspect) || return 1
  _tt_ok 'an interrupted pre-commit write is ignored and reported' _tt_contains "$result" 'ignored incomplete event files=1' || return 1
  _tt_call step >/dev/null || return 1
  _tt_ok 'continuation after an incomplete write adds one complete event' _tt_count 3 || return 1
  _tt_ok 'incomplete evidence is preserved' test -f "$fixture/events/.pending-interrupted" || return 1

  mkdir -- "$fixture/.writer-lock" || return 1
  lock_token="$$-11-12"
  print -r -- "$$|$lock_token" > "$fixture/.writer-lock/owner"
  _tt_ok 'a competing writer cannot enter' _tt_rejects step || return 1
  _tt_ok 'recovery requires the exact lock token' _tt_rejects recover wrong-token || return 1
  _tt_ok 'recovery refuses an extant owner process' _tt_rejects recover "$lock_token" || return 1
  print -r -- '99999999|99999999-11-12' > "$fixture/.writer-lock/owner"
  _tt_call recover 99999999-11-12 >/dev/null || return 1
  _tt_ok 'a dead writer can be explicitly recovered' test ! -e "$fixture/.writer-lock" || return 1
  mkdir -- "$fixture/.writer-lock" || return 1
  _tt_ok 'ownerless locks are not silently cleared' _tt_rejects step || return 1
  _tt_call recover owner-missing >/dev/null || return 1
  _tt_ok 'ownerless interruption has an explicit recovery path' test ! -e "$fixture/.writer-lock" || return 1

  original=$(<"$fixture/events/000001.receipt")
  print -r -- 'broken receipt' > "$fixture/events/000001.receipt"
  _tt_ok 'history corruption stops verification' _tt_rejects verify || return 1
  _tt_ok 'history corruption stops continuation' _tt_rejects step || return 1
  _tt_ok 'corrupt history is preserved for investigation' _tt_equal "$(<"$fixture/events/000001.receipt")" 'broken receipt' || return 1
  print -r -- "$original" > "$fixture/events/000001.receipt"
  fields=( "${(@s:|:)original}" )
  fields[5]=3
  body="${(j:|:)fields[1,7]}"
  # Load the helper without touching this fixture, then recompute a checksum for
  # an internally consistent but physically impossible forged result.
  . "$test_root/tendora.zsh" help >/dev/null || return 1
  _td_checksum "$body"
  print -r -- "$body|$REPLY" > "$fixture/events/000001.receipt"
  _tt_ok 'replay detects an impossible result even with a valid checksum' _tt_rejects verify || return 1
  print -r -- "$original" > "$fixture/events/000001.receipt"
  mv -- "$fixture/events/000001.receipt" "$fixture/saved.receipt" || return 1
  _tt_ok 'an interior gap stops verification' _tt_rejects verify || return 1
  mv -- "$fixture/saved.receipt" "$fixture/events/000001.receipt" || return 1
  print -r -- 'unexpected' > "$fixture/events/foreign-file"
  _tt_ok 'unexpected event material is refused' _tt_rejects verify || return 1
  rm -- "$fixture/events/foreign-file" || return 1
  id=$(_tt_call propose harvest) || return 1
  original=$(<"$fixture/proposals/$id.proposal")
  print -r -- "TENDORA-PROPOSAL/1|2|0|harvest" > "$fixture/proposals/$id.proposal"
  _tt_ok 'a proposal also pins the predecessor checksum' _tt_rejects commit "$id" || return 1
  print -r -- "$original" > "$fixture/proposals/$id.proposal"
  _tt_call commit "$id" >/dev/null || return 1
  result=$(_tt_call inspect) || return 1
  _tt_ok 'first harvest resumes from verified material' _tt_contains "$result" 'water=4/12 (reserve=2) beds=0/3 food=3/12' || return 1

  _tt_call run 20 >/dev/null || return 1
  result=$(_tt_call inspect) || return 1
  _tt_ok 'bounded continuation reaches its food goal' _tt_contains "$result" 'food=12/12' || return 1
  _tt_ok 'reaching the goal gives a visible pause' _tt_contains "$result" 'next=pause' || return 1
  _tt_ok 'the full replay has thirteen receipts' _tt_count 13 || return 1
  _tt_call step >/dev/null || return 1
  _tt_call run 20 >/dev/null || return 1
  _tt_ok 'continuation at the goal makes no further events' _tt_count 13 || return 1
  id=$(_tt_call propose collect) || return 1
  _tt_ok 'manual commits also respect the goal pause' _tt_rejects commit "$id" || return 1
  _tt_ok 'final history verifies' _tt_call verify || return 1

  rm -r -- "$fixture" || return 1
  print -r -- "PASS: $assertions assertions; isolated fixture removed"
}

_tt_main "$@"
